summary: The bill amends Medicare rules to distribute up to 2,000 new residency positions per year from 2026 through 2032 to qualifying hospitals, with one-third reserved for hospitals already over their caps, minimum shares for rural and shortage-area hospitals, and adjustments to indirect medical education payments.

scores.thoughts: The bill amends Medicare (title XVIII of the Social Security Act) to distribute up to 2,000 additional residency positions annually from FY2026–2032 (totaling 14,000 positions), with associated direct and indirect medical education payments to hospitals. This directly increases federal outlays under Medicare, expanding government spending on graduate medical education.
The bill contains no provisions related to taxes, tax rates, deductions, credits, or revenue measures.

The legislation increases the supply of physicians by expanding Medicare-funded residency slots, with priority for rural, HPSA, and certain teaching hospitals. While it operates through the existing Medicare payment system rather than creating new public coverage programs, it represents a federal intervention to address healthcare workforce shortages.
No provisions address firearms, gun regulations, or Second Amendment issues.
No provisions address immigration, visas, border security, or pathways to citizenship.
No provisions address reproductive health services, abortion access, or related regulations.
No provisions address military, defense, or national security spending or policy.
No provisions address environmental regulations, climate policy, or energy production.
The bill expands Medicare GME payments but does not alter eligibility, benefits, or funding levels for means-tested programs such as Medicaid, SNAP, TANF, or SSI.

The bill funds additional medical residency positions (post-graduate medical training) and includes a GAO study on workforce diversity. It does not address K-12 education, school choice, federal education funding formulas, or higher-education policy outside of GME.
No provisions address controlled substances, decriminalization, enforcement, or prescription drug regulation.
No provisions address sentencing, policing, incarceration, or criminal justice reform.
No provisions address tariffs, trade agreements, or import/export policy.
By increasing Medicare spending without offsetting revenue or cuts, the bill implicitly accepts additional deficit spending rather than prioritizing debt reduction.
No provisions address legal protections, nondiscrimination, or rights for LGBTQ+ individuals.
No provisions address foreign assistance, international aid, or State Department programs.
No provisions address voting access, election administration, or campaign finance.
No provisions address data privacy, technology regulation, or surveillance.
No provisions address collective bargaining, union rights, or labor standards.
No provisions address religious exemptions, conscience protections, or conflicts between civil rights and religious liberty.
